The long and short of it is your average emulator does not emulate the hardware but only tries replicate the necessary functions of the hardware right as they are needed. This is called just in time / JIT or dynamic recompilation. Its the only known way for most hardware to be emulated successfully at playable speeds but you have to have an encyclopedic knowledge of the hardware to pull it off.

This dynamic recompilation isn't always accurate enough for every game to be playable or emulated accurately because of how the internal behavior of the GameCube / Wii CPU and or GPU can manipulate calculations in ways that are not always 100% understood. A simple example is how floating point numbers (numbers like PI etc) are stored and manipulated. http://wiibrew.org/wiki/Paired_single here is a really nice example of how the processor has its own way of handling this kind of stuff.

A more complicated example would be how Sin and Cos are calculated, that kind of trigonometric math is incredibly important for 3D so that in combination with floating point numbers is how you get accurate three dimensional perspectives. Then you've got the Z-buffer which is basically an internal register (memory space) of the GPU that is used to store and manipulate depth information in a 3D scene, the thing about the Z-buffer is its pretty much essential if you want to do particle FX (fogging, sparks, flames etc), stencil shadows (the shadows you see in most games are calculated by duplicating the polygon model then calculating the perspective of the light source and figuring out how to flatten the duplicated "shadow" model so it wraps onto the object / terrain), intelligent scene culling (the process where the back of an object / piece of terrain isn't rendered to save processing power because from the cameras perspective it is not visible), and finally to end this little Z buffer rant the render order of a scene as in figuring out which building is in front of which in a city. All of this is done for every single frame that is rendered, if your emulator gets it wrong then your game might be unplayable (spiderman2 in the video) and extremely inaccurate (Rogue Squadron in the video).

Working this stuff out, testing and micro patching games, preforming substitutions and replacements of instructions kind of stuff is why you don't need a super computer to play emulated games. Dolphin 5.0 is a tour-de-force in reverse engineering and computer science.
